statement: Modern critical scholarship commonly models early Israelite religion as developing at least partly within the Canaanite cultural-religious matrix rather than as an initially isolated system wholly separate from its Levantine neighbors.

sources.citation: Mark S. Smith, The Early History of God: Yahweh and the Other Deities in Ancient Israel, 2nd ed. (Eerdmans, 2002).
sources.author: Mark S. Smith
sources.access_note: Publisher summary explicitly states that Israelite religion developed, at least in part, from Canaanite religion and rejects a clean initial cultural-religious separation.

sources.citation: Theodore J. Lewis, The Origin and Character of God (Oxford University Press, 2020), chs. 4 and 6.
sources.author: Theodore J. Lewis
sources.access_note: Oxford abstracts explicitly treat El worship, Yahweh's origins, and a Canaanite cultural continuum through the Late Bronze and Iron Ages.

does_not_demonstrate: This does not mean every Israelite community practiced the same religion.
This does not establish that Yahweh himself originated as a Canaanite deity.
This does not turn every Canaanite-Israelite similarity into a borrowing event.
adversarial_counter: Yahweh may have had a distinct southern origin; cultural continuity in Israel does not require Yahweh's own ultimate origin to be Canaanite.
notes: Backs the tradition-level CULTURAL_FUSION relationship while preserving the separate southern-origin question.
